say.text: Booking clerk: a 23-year-old has found a new breast lump and wants the first scan booked.
Which imaging do you book first?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Under 35 the breast is dense, so ultrasound is the preferred first imaging.
Not right. Mammography is the usual first test over about 35 to 40, so it feels like the default.
Under 35 the breast is dense, and ultrasound is the preferred first imaging there.
Right: breast ultrasound, which also separates solid from cystic lesions.
Not quite. MRI sounds thorough, and it has a role in extent and high-risk women.
It is not the first test for a lump in a 23-year-old. Ultrasound is.
Check her age first. Think about which test suits older women, and which works in a young, dense breast.
A 50-year-old has a 2 cm hard breast lump. Before surgery the team needs to know if it is invasive, and its ER, PR and HER2 status.
Which sample do you send?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Core needle biopsy gives invasive or in situ status, grade, and ER, PR and HER2 status.
Not right. FNAC is the test older papers expected, so it feels like the classic answer.
FNAC gives cells, not tissue, so it cannot show invasion or give ER, PR and HER2 status.
Right: core needle biopsy. FNAC is kept for axillary nodes and cysts.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: FNAC is still printed in old keys. Current practice is core biopsy.

say.text: Not quite. Excision removes the lump as surgery, before anyone knows the tumour type.
A core needle biopsy gives the invasive status and receptors before any operation.
Think about what the pathologist must report: whether the tumour invades, and its receptor status. Which sample keeps the tissue?
A 44-year-old has a 1.8 cm node-negative invasive carcinoma. No bone pain, normal liver tests, no symptoms.
Which distant staging do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Early, asymptomatic disease needs no routine metastatic work-up.
Not right. Bone is the commonest site of spread, so a bone scan feels like routine staging.
Routine imaging is not needed in early asymptomatic disease. Scans are for locally advanced disease or symptoms.
Right: no routine metastatic work-up here, so plan local treatment.
Not quite. PET-CT feels thorough, but routine metastatic imaging is not needed in early asymptomatic disease.
Reserve staging scans for locally advanced disease or symptoms.
Ask what a distant scan would change. Would it alter the plan for an early patient with no symptoms?
Tumour board: a 7 cm breast cancer with bulky axillary nodes and no distant spread.
Which treatment comes first?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy shrinks the tumour and is the first step for locally advanced disease.
Not right. Starting with the mastectomy feels natural, since it removes the disease.
In locally advanced disease, chemotherapy comes first to shrink the tumour before the operation.
Right: for inflammatory or locally advanced cancer the order is chemotherapy, then MRM, then radiotherapy.
Not quite. Radiotherapy is part of the plan, but not as the first step for a bulky tumour.
The trimodality pathway puts radiotherapy after the mastectomy.
Ask what this tumour needs before any operation. Would surgery first control it?
A woman has a 1.6 cm invasive cancer. The axilla is clinically node-negative.
Which rule do you apply to the axilla?

choices.label: Dissect first; sentinel node only if that fails
Radiotherapy to the axilla with no sampling
Sentinel node biopsy; dissect only if positive
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Sentinel node biopsy stages a clinically node-negative axilla; dissection follows only if it is positive.
Not right. Clearing the armpit first feels like the thorough, classic step, so it is tempting.
In a clinically node-negative axilla, sentinel node biopsy stages the nodes. Full dissection is for a positive node.
Right: sentinel node biopsy first, and dissect only if the node is positive.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: dissecting first is the old order, and older papers still print it.

say.text: Not quite. Radiotherapy does not stage the axilla, so you lose the nodal result a biopsy gives.
Sentinel node biopsy comes first, and dissection follows only if it is positive.
Ask whether the axilla must be cleared to be staged, or whether one node can answer the question.
A 45-year-old on tamoxifen for 3 years has abnormal uterine bleeding.
Your first move?

choices.label: Reassure her; tamoxifen protects the endometrium
Urgent endometrial assessment before anything else
Switch to an aromatase inhibitor without examining the uterus

say.text: Yes. Tamoxifen can cause endometrial carcinoma, so bleeding needs endometrial assessment first.
Not right. Tamoxifen acts as an antagonist in the breast, so it seems protective everywhere. That is the tempting leap.
In the endometrium it acts as an oestrogen agonist and raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma.
Right: assess the endometrium urgently, because bleeding on tamoxifen can be cancer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: tamoxifen does not protect the uterus, whatever it does in the breast.

say.text: Not quite. Switching drugs is a later decision, and it is tempting as the tamoxifen fix.
First exclude endometrial carcinoma, which tamoxifen can cause. The uterus comes before the drug change.
The team says a 6 cm tumour rules out breast conservation on size alone.
Your reply?

choices.label: Right: a tumour above 5 cm is a contraindication to BCS
Judged against breast size, BCS may still be possible
Shrinkage after chemotherapy makes margins unreliable

say.text: Yes. Size is judged against the breast, and BCS may still be possible if margins and radiotherapy can be achieved.
Not right. A 5 cm cut-off is easy to remember, so size looks like a hard rule.
Size is a relative factor, judged against the breast. Poor cosmesis is a relative reason, not an absolute bar.
Right: BCS can be offered when clear margins and whole-breast radiotherapy are feasible.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: size is a relative factor, and the absolute reasons are about margins and radiotherapy.

say.text: Not quite. Chemotherapy shrinkage is a reason to consider conservation, not a reason to refuse it.
Downstaging an operable tumour is done to allow BCS.
Which statement about nerve injury after axillary clearance is right?

choices.label: Long thoracic nerve injury is the commonest, causing winging
Intercostobrachial injury is commonest, causing medial arm numbness
Thoracodorsal injury weakens the latissimus dorsi

say.text: Yes. Intercostobrachial injury is the commonest, giving numbness of the medial upper arm.
Not right. Winging is the most dramatic deficit, so it feels like the commonest one.
Long thoracic nerve injury does cause winging, but it is not the commonest injury in axillary clearance.
The commonest is the intercostobrachial nerve, giving numbness of the medial upper arm.
Not quite. Thoracodorsal injury is real, and it weakens latissimus dorsi.
But it is not the commonest injury. That is the intercostobrachial nerve.
A man with breast cancer has a germline change found on genetic testing.
Which gene is most likely?
Yes. BRCA2 is the gene most associated with male breast cancer, alongside Klinefelter syndrome.
Not right. BRCA1 is the famous breast cancer gene, so it feels like the answer for everyone.
BRCA1 is linked to triple-negative cancers in women. In men the link is to BRCA2.
Right: BRCA2 is the gene more associated with male breast cancer.
Not quite. PTEN belongs to a different syndrome, not to male breast cancer.
The gene linked to male breast cancer is BRCA2.
An operable cancer is not suited to breast conservation. The plan should name:

choices.label: Simple mastectomy with no axillary surgery

say.text: Yes. MRM removes the breast and axillary nodes and keeps pectoralis major, unlike Halsted.
Not right. Halsted is the classic, most radical option, so it feels like the safe standard.
Halsted removes pectoralis major and minor and all axillary levels. It is now rarely done.
Right: modified radical mastectomy, which keeps pectoralis major. Older keys gave Halsted as standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the old key named Halsted, and current practice names MRM or BCS.

say.text: Not quite. Simple mastectomy leaves the axilla unplanned, and that is not the standard for an operable cancer.
Early breast cancer needs surgery to the breast and the axilla, with radiotherapy and systemic therapy as indicated.

cards.q: Which tissue test does a breast lump need, and why?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy, because it shows invasion and ER, PR and HER2 status. FNAC is kept for nodes and cysts.

cards.q: Does early, asymptomatic breast cancer need routine metastatic imaging?
cards.a: No. Metastatic imaging is for locally advanced disease or symptoms.

cards.q: Which operation is the current standard for an operable cancer not suited to BCS?
cards.a: Modified radical mastectomy, which keeps pectoralis major. Halsted is rarely done now.

cards.q: What is the axillary plan for a clinically node-negative invasive cancer?
cards.a: Sentinel node biopsy first, and dissection only if the sentinel node is positive.

cards.q: What is the order of treatment for inflammatory carcinoma?
cards.a: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then MRM, then post-mastectomy radiotherapy.

cards.q: Why does a woman on tamoxifen with bleeding need an endometrial check?
cards.a: Tamoxifen can cause endometrial carcinoma. Raloxifene does not raise endometrial cancer risk.

cards.q: Which nerve is most often injured in axillary dissection, and what does it cause?
cards.a: The intercostobrachial nerve, causing numbness of the medial upper arm.
